screens.title: What are Materials and Textures?
screens.narratorSegment: Materials are collections of shader parameters and texture references that define how a surface responds to light. A material holds references to texture maps such as the Albedo (color), Normal (surface direction), Metallic and Smoothness maps. Textures are image files that supply pixel data for those channels. Together, a material plus textures produce the final look on a mesh. For example, a wooden crate material uses an Albedo map for color and a Normal map to simulate grain without adding geometry. This separation of shader logic and image data is important: changing the Normal map changes surface detail while the geometry remains unchanged. A common misconception is that textures automatically become editable materials on import: embedded materials inside an FBX are created as part of the import but are not editable until you extract them. Another misconception is that all textures are color images; some textures are data maps and must not use sRGB color conversion. Real-world significance: if you set a normal map as a color texture, lighting will be wrong and fine surface detail will disappear. Takeaway: treat materials as containers and textures as data — configure each texture type to match its role and extract materials when you need control.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › What are Materials and Textures?
Definition

Materials vs Textures

A material holds shader properties and links to textures. Textures are images that supply color or data to those properties.

Albedo (Color)
Represents the base color of the surface and should use sRGB.
Normal Map
Stores surface normals as vectors and must be treated as a data texture with sRGB disabled.
Concrete Example
Imagine a wooden crate: the Albedo map paints the wood grain color, the Normal map fakes deep grain and scratches, and the Metallic/smoothness maps control how shiny parts of the crate appear. No extra polygons are needed to show dents or grain when the normal map is correct.
Key Takeaway
Treat textures by role: color vs data. This preserves lighting and color accuracy.
Common Mistake
Setting a normal map as a color texture causes flat, incorrect lighting and broken surface detail.

screens.title: Materials Tab & Material Creation Mode
screens.narratorSegment: When you select an imported model, the Inspector exposes a Materials tab that controls how Unity handles materials related to that file. The central setting is Material Creation Mode. If you choose "From Model's Material," Unity attempts to recreate the materials defined in your FBX using embedded names and properties. This is convenient when your DCC tool has already assigned meaningful material names. If you choose a built-in option such as "PBR (Physically Based Rendering)" or "Standard (Legacy)," Unity will force new materials that use those shaders and default parameter mappings. Use PBR for modern realistic lighting. Choosing "None" tells Unity not to create materials during import; this is useful when you maintain a curated material library in Unity and want to assign assets manually. Material Search works together with creation mode: searching by Base Texture Name or Material Name helps Unity link to existing materials in the project instead of creating duplicates. A common misconception is that letting Unity auto-create materials always saves time. In large projects it can proliferate redundant materials. Example: if you import a modular building set and auto-create, you may produce dozens of near-duplicate materials; searching by base texture name or using "None" and manually assigning your canonical materials keeps your asset library tidy. Takeaway: pick the creation mode to match your pipeline and use Material Search to reduce duplication.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Materials Tab & Material Creation Mode
Definition & Modes

Material Creation Mode

Options include "From Model's Material", "PBR (Physically Based Rendering)", "Standard (Legacy)", and "None". Each affects whether Unity generates materials and which shader defaults are used.
From Model's Material
Recreates materials from the FBX metadata. Best when your DCC names and sets materials consistently.
PBR / Standard
Forces materials to use Unity PBR or Standard shader; useful when you want consistent shader behavior across assets.
None
Prevents material creation. Use when you control material assignment manually from a project library.
Practical Example
If you import a modular environment set and allow auto-creation, Unity often produces separate materials per mesh leading to many similar materials. Instead, set Material Search to match by base texture name or set creation to "None" and assign your canonical materials. This keeps the project clean and ensures shader parameters remain consistent.
Check
After import, look in Project window for duplicated .mat files to verify your search settings worked.
Mistake
Relying on default creation in large projects leads to scattered material variants that are hard to maintain.

screens.title: Extracting Materials and Textures
screens.narratorSegment: Embedded materials and textures in an FBX are convenient during export, but they are not editable as standalone Unity assets until you extract them. The Extract workflow is simple and powerful. When you click "Extract Materials..." Unity prompts you to choose a folder—create a dedicated Assets/Materials folder for organization. Unity then creates. mat files for each embedded material. Extracting textures similarly creates image files in your project. Why extract? Extracted assets become regular Unity assets you can open, edit, assign different shaders, tweak metallic or smoothness sliders, or swap textures without re-exporting from your DCC. A concrete example: you import a character with embedded materials and want to replace the skin shader or adjust roughness. If the materials are embedded, you must re-export; after extraction, you can directly change shader properties in the Inspector. A common misconception is that extraction duplicates assets unnecessarily. Proper organization prevents duplication: extract into a dedicated folder, inspect and delete unused files, and use Material Search to link to existing assets when possible. Takeaway: extract when you need control, and organize extracted assets so they integrate into your project library.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Extracting Materials and Textures
Step-by-step
  1. Select the imported FBX in Project window and open the Materials tab in the Inspector.
  2. Click "Extract Materials..." and choose a folder such as Assets/Materials to save .mat files.
  3. Locate the created .mat files and open them to change shader properties or assign different textures.
  4. For textures, use "Extract Textures..." to generate image files you can set Texture Import Settings on.
Best Practice
Extract into organized folders and remove duplicates; this keeps your project assets clean and editable.
Concrete Scenario
You import a vehicle with embedded materials but want to use a specific car paint shader in Unity. Extract the materials, open the .mat, switch to your paint shader, and tweak metallic and smoothness until it matches the desired look—no DCC re-export required.
Check
Verify that extracted textures are referenced by the .mat and accessible in Project window.
Pitfall
Extracting into many scattered folders creates maintenance headaches; consolidate extracted assets.

screens.title: Texture Import Settings — Overview
screens.narratorSegment: Each texture file in Unity has Texture Import Settings accessible via the Inspector. These settings determine how the image data is interpreted and optimized. Key fields include Texture Type, sRGB (Color Texture), Generate Mip Maps, Compression, Wrap Mode, Filter Mode, and Aniso Level. Texture Type tells Unity how to treat the file: Default for color maps like Albedo, Normal Map for surface normals, Sprite for UI, and Lightmap for baked lighting. sRGB should be enabled for color textures so Unity performs correct color space conversion; it must be disabled for data maps like normal and metallic where channel values are not colors. Mip Maps provide pre-calculated scaled versions of the texture to prevent shimmering and to reduce G P U workload at distance; usually enabled for 3D textures. Compression reduces memory footprint but can introduce artifacts—pick the scheme and quality appropriate to the platform. Wrap Mode controls tiling behavior, Filter Mode controls sampling when scaled, and Aniso Level improves quality at glancing angles. A common misconception is to treat every texture the same: instead, match settings to the texture’s role and the art direction. Example: UI icons often need no mip maps and point filtering to remain crisp; 3D albedo maps benefit from mips and trilinear filtering. Takeaway: inspect each texture and choose settings that preserve intended look while optimizing performance.

keyIdea.text: Match Texture Type to role, enable sRGB for color, enable mip maps for 3D textures, and choose compression appropriate to platform and alpha usage.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Texture Import Settings — Overview
Primary Settings
Texture Type
Default, Normal Map, Sprite, Lightmap, HDR. Choose the one that matches texture purpose.
sRGB (Color Texture)
Enable for Albedo; disable for data textures like normals, metallic, or height maps.
Generate Mip Maps
Enable for 3D textures to improve visual stability and reduce GPU bandwidth at distance.
Support & Examples
UI sprite: Texture Type = Sprite, sRGB enabled, mip maps disabled, point or bilinear filter for crisp pixels. Normal map: Texture Type = Normal Map, sRGB disabled to preserve vector data. Albedo: Default with sRGB enabled, mips on, and platform compression as appropriate.
Key Takeaway
Every texture needs role-based settings; a one-size-fits-all approach causes visual or performance problems.
Common Mistake
Leaving Normal Maps as Default and sRGB enabled breaks lighting calculations and surface detail.

screens.title: Normal Maps: Data Textures and sRGB
screens.narratorSegment: Normal maps store surface direction vectors per pixel, not color information. These vectors tell the shader how light should reflect across a surface to simulate bumps and grooves without extra geometry. Because normal maps represent direction data, they must be imported as a Normal Map texture type and have sRGB disabled. sRGB performs a gamma-correct color conversion intended for display colors; applying it to vector data distorts the numeric values and ruins lighting. A concrete scenario: you import a metal grate and set the normal as Default with sRGB enabled; the surface will look flat or have strange shading. Correct import—Texture Type set to Normal Map and sRGB disabled—ensures the normal vectors are interpreted linearly and lighting remains accurate. Another important point: Unity may apply special compression or packing for normal maps when the type is set correctly to preserve direction precision. A common misconception is assuming normal maps are simply tinted images; in practice they require permissions to be treated as data. Takeaway: always set normal maps to Normal Map and disable sRGB to preserve lighting integrity. Normal Maps: Data Textures and sRGB means set texture type to normal map and disable srgb so unity reads the map as vector data and preserves correct lighting.. In practical terms, why normal maps are not color images and how to import them correctly. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Normal Maps: Data Textures and sRGB
Definition

Normal Map = vector data

Normal maps encode x/y/z direction per pixel. They are not colors and must avoid sRGB conversion to remain numerically correct.

Quick Rule
Texture Type: Normal Map. sRGB: Disabled. This preserves lighting calculations.
Concrete Example
If a terrain tile looks flat after import, inspect the normal map settings. If you see sRGB enabled or Texture Type set to Default, switch to Normal Map and disable sRGB, then click Apply to restore correct surface detail.
Check
Apply the texture to a material and move lights around to confirm the normal detail responds as expected.
Misconception
Treating normal maps as colors will cause incorrect shading; they must be linear data.

screens.title: Mip Maps: Purpose and When to Use Them
screens.narratorSegment: Mip maps are pre-generated, scaled-down versions of a texture used when the textured surface appears small on-screen. They reduce aliasing and shimmering by providing lower-resolution versions that match the rendered size, and they reduce G P U memory bandwidth because the G P U can sample a smaller mip level for distant geometry. Enable Generate Mip Maps for most 3D textures; this improves visual quality and performance. Exceptions include UI elements, pixel art, or cases where you require the texture to remain crisp at all distances—disabling mip maps keeps the full-resolution sample but can cause aliasing and increased bandwidth usage. A concrete example: a floor tile far from the camera without mip maps may shimmer and stress memory; enabling mips provides stable, lower-resolution textures and smoother rendering. A common misconception is that mip maps always reduce memory; in reality they increase total texture storage slightly but save runtime bandwidth and improve perceived performance. Takeaway: prefer mip maps for 3D textures where distance-based sampling occurs; disable only for intentional crispness in UI or pixel art. content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Mip Maps: Purpose and When to Use Them
Why Mip Maps

Reduce aliasing and bandwidth

Mip maps provide smaller precomputed versions of a texture so GPUs can sample an appropriate level. They prevent shimmering and save bandwidth at distance.

When to enable
Enable for most 3D surface textures like terrain, props, and characters. Disable for UI and pixel art.
Concrete Example
A distant city wall without mip maps will exhibit aliasing and cause the GPU to sample full-resolution texture repeatedly. Enabling mip maps gives the GPU smaller textures to use at distance and reduces both aliasing and bandwidth.
Key Takeaway
Mips improve stability and performance; prefer them for 3D assets.
Exception
Disable for UI sprites or pixel-art where mip smoothing would blur desired sharp edges.

screens.title: Texture Compression & Platform Choices
screens.narratorSegment: Texture compression reduces file size and runtime memory at the cost of some visual quality. The main idea is to pick formats suited to each platform and texture needs. On desktop you might use DXT1 for textures without alpha and DXT5 for those with alpha. Mobile devices use formats like PVRTC, ETC, or ASTC. ASTC offers high-quality results with flexible block sizes but may not be available on older devices. Compression settings include quality sliders such as None, Normal, and High Quality. None preserves maximum fidelity but consumes the most memory, while Normal and High compress progressively more. Always test compressed results visually because compression artifacts sometimes appear on fine detail or normal maps. For normal maps, ensure your texture type is Normal Map so Unity uses appropriate compression. A common mistake is leaving all textures uncompressed; this inflates build size and memory use dramatically. Another mistake is using a single compression choice across platforms. Example: choose DXT5 for desktop albedo with alpha, and ASTC 6x6 for modern mobile for a good balance. Takeaway: use platform overrides and quality testing to find the right compromise between fidelity and performance for each target platform.

screens.title: Wrap Mode, Filter Mode & Aniso Level
screens.narratorSegment: Wrap Mode, Filter Mode, and Aniso Level control how a texture is sampled and displayed when UVs go beyond the 0-to-1 range or when viewed at oblique angles. Wrap Mode has common options Repeat and Clamp. Repeat tiles the texture across UV coordinates, while Clamp stretches the edges. Use Repeat for tiled surfaces like floors and walls; use Clamp for decals or single-use textures. Filter Mode affects how pixels blend when scaling: Point preserves a pixelated look, Bilinear smooths between texels, and Trilinear improves transitions between mip levels. Aniso Level improves sampling quality at glancing angles, especially important for ground textures viewed horizontally. Increasing Aniso Level produces crisper textures at a cost in sampling performance. A common misconception is that increasing Anisotropic filtering is free—on mobile hardware it has a cost. Example: a terrain material benefits from Aniso Level 4–8 to keep grass textures readable at a distance, while small decals can use point filtering. Takeaway: choose Wrap and Filter modes based on aesthetic needs, and use Aniso only where angle-based quality matters. Wrap Mode, Filter Mode & Aniso Level means use repeat for tiled surfaces, choose filters per aesthetic, and increase aniso for oblique-angle clarity when needed.. In practical terms, controls for sampling, tiling, and angle-based quality. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. screens.title: Hands-on: Import, Extract, Configure, Validate
screens.narratorSegment: Follow a short workflow to practice material and texture import settings. Step one: import a simple FBX that has an Albedo and a Normal map embedded or referenced. Step two: open the Materials tab and inspect Material Creation Mode and Material Search. If the file embeds materials you plan to edit, click "Extract Materials..." and place them in Assets/Materials. Step three: locate the extracted textures and set the Albedo texture Texture Type to Default and enable sRGB. For the Normal map set Texture Type to Normal Map and disable sRGB. Assign the material to a simple sphere and move the directional light to ensure normals and color render as expected.

Remember to apply changes in the Inspector. If the normal map still looks wrong, re-open the texture, confirm Texture Type, and ensure sRGB is disabled. Organize extracted assets into predictable folders to avoid accidental duplicates.

Use a standard test geometry like a sphere to compare material changes quickly.

Forgetting to disable sRGB on normal maps is the most frequent reason for poor normal map results.

screens.title: Common Import Mistakes and How to Fix Them
screens.narratorSegment: Knowing the common mistakes helps you troubleshoot quickly. First, not extracting materials locks them inside the FBX so you cannot edit shader properties; the fix is to Extract Materials into an organized folder and reassign as needed. Second, incorrect Texture Type for normal maps—leaving them as Default with sRGB enabled—produces incorrect lighting; set Texture Type to Normal Map and disable sRGB. Third, disabling mip maps on 3D textures causes shimmering and aliasing; re-enable mip generation for those textures. Fourth, using no compression everywhere dramatically increases build size; choose compression per platform and test to find acceptable visual trade-offs. Fifth, mismatched naming conventions prevent Material Search from linking textures and materials automatically; adopt consistent base texture and material names in your DCC pipeline. A concrete example: if your imported asset shows dull surfaces where metallic or roughness maps exist, inspect whether those maps were imported with the correct Texture Type and sRGB settings, and whether the material references them after extraction. Takeaway: follow the extract, configure, test loop to recover from most import issues. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you will learn how Unity brings your 3D art to life by processing materials and textures during import. Materials define how a surface reacts to light, and textures are the images that provide color, surface detail, and other data. Together they determine whether a model looks realistic and whether your project runs efficiently. We will examine Unity’s Materials tab on an imported model, the choices for Material Creation Mode, and how Material Search links or creates assets. You’ll also see why extracting embedded materials and textures is a best practice so you can edit them freely. For textures we will cover the Texture Type options, sRGB usage, mip maps, compression choices, and settings like wrap and filter mode. Each of these affects visual result and memory use. For example, a normal map must be set as a Normal Map type with sRGB disabled to preserve vector data; otherwise lighting will be wrong. By mastering these import settings you gain precise control over look and performance. Consider a simple crate asset: correct import settings can turn a flat box into a believable object with subtle surface relief while keeping memory low. As you move through the lesson, notice the concrete steps you can apply immediately in your project.

These objectives map to practical skills you can use immediately. First, you will be able to describe how Unity handles materials and textures for imported models, which means knowing what the Materials tab controls and how Unity decides to recreate or search for materials. Second, you will configure the Material Import Settings: set Material Creation Mode, choose a Material Search strategy, and extract embedded assets so they become editable. Third, you will apply correct Texture Import Settings: choose texture types like Default or Normal Map, set sRGB appropriately, enable mip maps when needed, and pick compression levels that fit your target platform. Finally, you will develop an inspection workflow to test visual results after changing import settings so you can spot incorrect normal maps, missing albedo color space settings, or inefficient compression choices. Each objective combines a definition, a hands-on action, and a reason why it matters so you can act confidently in your projects.

These additional objectives focus on concrete actions you will take while importing assets. You will learn to choose the appropriate Material Creation Mode: whether to let Unity recreate from the model, force PBR/Standard, or prevent automatic creation when you want a curated material library. You will learn Material Search strategies such as searching by material name or base texture name to reuse existing assets and avoid duplication. You will practice setting Texture Compression and platform overrides so textures are tailored for PC, mobile, or other targets. Finally, you will identify when to disable mip maps—for UI or pixel-art textures—to avoid unwanted blurring. Each objective includes the reason it matters: control over creation maintains asset hygiene, search reduces duplication, compression cuts memory usage, and mip decisions protect visual intent. Use these objectives as a checklist for every imported model.

Materials are collections of shader parameters and texture references that define how a surface responds to light. A material holds references to texture maps such as the Albedo (color), Normal (surface direction), Metallic and Smoothness maps. Textures are image files that supply pixel data for those channels. Together, a material plus textures produce the final look on a mesh. For example, a wooden crate material uses an Albedo map for color and a Normal map to simulate grain without adding geometry. This separation of shader logic and image data is important: changing the Normal map changes surface detail while the geometry remains unchanged. A common misconception is that textures automatically become editable materials on import: embedded materials inside an FBX are created as part of the import but are not editable until you extract them. Another misconception is that all textures are color images; some textures are data maps and must not use sRGB color conversion. Real-world significance: if you set a normal map as a color texture, lighting will be wrong and fine surface detail will disappear. Takeaway: treat materials as containers and textures as data — configure each texture type to match its role and extract materials when you need control.

When you select an imported model, the Inspector exposes a Materials tab that controls how Unity handles materials related to that file. The central setting is Material Creation Mode. If you choose "From Model's Material," Unity attempts to recreate the materials defined in your FBX using embedded names and properties. This is convenient when your DCC tool has already assigned meaningful material names. If you choose a built-in option such as "PBR (Physically Based Rendering)" or "Standard (Legacy)," Unity will force new materials that use those shaders and default parameter mappings. Use PBR for modern realistic lighting. Choosing "None" tells Unity not to create materials during import; this is useful when you maintain a curated material library in Unity and want to assign assets manually. Material Search works together with creation mode: searching by Base Texture Name or Material Name helps Unity link to existing materials in the project instead of creating duplicates. A common misconception is that letting Unity auto-create materials always saves time. In large projects it can proliferate redundant materials. Example: if you import a modular building set and auto-create, you may produce dozens of near-duplicate materials; searching by base texture name or using "None" and manually assigning your canonical materials keeps your asset library tidy. Takeaway: pick the creation mode to match your pipeline and use Material Search to reduce duplication.

Embedded materials and textures in an FBX are convenient during export, but they are not editable as standalone Unity assets until you extract them. The Extract workflow is simple and powerful. When you click "Extract Materials..." Unity prompts you to choose a folder—create a dedicated Assets/Materials folder for organization. Unity then creates. mat files for each embedded material. Extracting textures similarly creates image files in your project. Why extract? Extracted assets become regular Unity assets you can open, edit, assign different shaders, tweak metallic or smoothness sliders, or swap textures without re-exporting from your DCC. A concrete example: you import a character with embedded materials and want to replace the skin shader or adjust roughness. If the materials are embedded, you must re-export; after extraction, you can directly change shader properties in the Inspector. A common misconception is that extraction duplicates assets unnecessarily. Proper organization prevents duplication: extract into a dedicated folder, inspect and delete unused files, and use Material Search to link to existing assets when possible. Takeaway: extract when you need control, and organize extracted assets so they integrate into your project library.

Each texture file in Unity has Texture Import Settings accessible via the Inspector. These settings determine how the image data is interpreted and optimized. Key fields include Texture Type, sRGB (Color Texture), Generate Mip Maps, Compression, Wrap Mode, Filter Mode, and Aniso Level. Texture Type tells Unity how to treat the file: Default for color maps like Albedo, Normal Map for surface normals, Sprite for UI, and Lightmap for baked lighting. sRGB should be enabled for color textures so Unity performs correct color space conversion; it must be disabled for data maps like normal and metallic where channel values are not colors. Mip Maps provide pre-calculated scaled versions of the texture to prevent shimmering and to reduce G P U workload at distance; usually enabled for 3D textures. Compression reduces memory footprint but can introduce artifacts—pick the scheme and quality appropriate to the platform. Wrap Mode controls tiling behavior, Filter Mode controls sampling when scaled, and Aniso Level improves quality at glancing angles. A common misconception is to treat every texture the same: instead, match settings to the texture’s role and the art direction. Example: UI icons often need no mip maps and point filtering to remain crisp; 3D albedo maps benefit from mips and trilinear filtering. Takeaway: inspect each texture and choose settings that preserve intended look while optimizing performance.

Normal maps store surface direction vectors per pixel, not color information. These vectors tell the shader how light should reflect across a surface to simulate bumps and grooves without extra geometry. Because normal maps represent direction data, they must be imported as a Normal Map texture type and have sRGB disabled. sRGB performs a gamma-correct color conversion intended for display colors; applying it to vector data distorts the numeric values and ruins lighting. A concrete scenario: you import a metal grate and set the normal as Default with sRGB enabled; the surface will look flat or have strange shading. Correct import—Texture Type set to Normal Map and sRGB disabled—ensures the normal vectors are interpreted linearly and lighting remains accurate. Another important point: Unity may apply special compression or packing for normal maps when the type is set correctly to preserve direction precision. A common misconception is assuming normal maps are simply tinted images; in practice they require permissions to be treated as data. Takeaway: always set normal maps to Normal Map and disable sRGB to preserve lighting integrity. Normal Maps: Data Textures and sRGB means set texture type to normal map and disable srgb so unity reads the map as vector data and preserves correct lighting.. In practical terms, why normal maps are not color images and how to import them correctly. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Mip maps are pre-generated, scaled-down versions of a texture used when the textured surface appears small on-screen. They reduce aliasing and shimmering by providing lower-resolution versions that match the rendered size, and they reduce G P U memory bandwidth because the G P U can sample a smaller mip level for distant geometry. Enable Generate Mip Maps for most 3D textures; this improves visual quality and performance. Exceptions include UI elements, pixel art, or cases where you require the texture to remain crisp at all distances—disabling mip maps keeps the full-resolution sample but can cause aliasing and increased bandwidth usage. A concrete example: a floor tile far from the camera without mip maps may shimmer and stress memory; enabling mips provides stable, lower-resolution textures and smoother rendering. A common misconception is that mip maps always reduce memory; in reality they increase total texture storage slightly but save runtime bandwidth and improve perceived performance. Takeaway: prefer mip maps for 3D textures where distance-based sampling occurs; disable only for intentional crispness in UI or pixel art. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Texture compression reduces file size and runtime memory at the cost of some visual quality. The main idea is to pick formats suited to each platform and texture needs. On desktop you might use DXT1 for textures without alpha and DXT5 for those with alpha. Mobile devices use formats like PVRTC, ETC, or ASTC. ASTC offers high-quality results with flexible block sizes but may not be available on older devices. Compression settings include quality sliders such as None, Normal, and High Quality. None preserves maximum fidelity but consumes the most memory, while Normal and High compress progressively more. Always test compressed results visually because compression artifacts sometimes appear on fine detail or normal maps. For normal maps, ensure your texture type is Normal Map so Unity uses appropriate compression. A common mistake is leaving all textures uncompressed; this inflates build size and memory use dramatically. Another mistake is using a single compression choice across platforms. Example: choose DXT5 for desktop albedo with alpha, and ASTC 6x6 for modern mobile for a good balance. Takeaway: use platform overrides and quality testing to find the right compromise between fidelity and performance for each target platform.

Wrap Mode has common options Repeat and Clamp. Repeat tiles the texture across UV coordinates, while Clamp stretches the edges. Use Repeat for tiled surfaces like floors and walls; use Clamp for decals or single-use textures. Filter Mode affects how pixels blend when scaling: Point preserves a pixelated look, Bilinear smooths between texels, and Trilinear improves transitions between mip levels. Aniso Level improves sampling quality at glancing angles, especially important for ground textures viewed horizontally. Increasing Aniso Level produces crisper textures at a cost in sampling performance. A common misconception is that increasing Anisotropic filtering is free—on mobile hardware it has a cost. Knowing the common mistakes helps you troubleshoot quickly. First, not extracting materials locks them inside the FBX so you cannot edit shader properties; the fix is to Extract Materials into an organized folder and reassign as needed. Second, incorrect Texture Type for normal maps—leaving them as Default with sRGB enabled—produces incorrect lighting; set Texture Type to Normal Map and disable sRGB. Third, disabling mip maps on 3D textures causes shimmering and aliasing; re-enable mip generation for those textures. Fourth, using no compression everywhere dramatically increases build size; choose compression per platform and test to find acceptable visual trade-offs.
